<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par132 />{{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=20|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים}}= ''another god'', and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=24|verse=19}} {{GHGheb|text=אֱלֹהִים קְדֹשִׁים}} (but cf. above, {{GHGpar|124|g}}–{{GHGpar|124|k|nonumber=1}}). On the other hand, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=4|verse=8}} is to be explained as having been said by the Philistines, who supposed that the Israelites had several gods. On the connexion of {{GHGheb|text=אֱלֹהִים}} with a plural predicate, see {{GHGpar|145|i}}.

'''2.''' On the adjective (in the construct state) governing a following genitive, see {{GHGpar|128|x}}; for the participle in the same construction, see {{GHGpar|116|f}}–''l''.<section end=par132 />

<section begin=par133 />{{GHGpar-heading|133|The Comparison of Adjectives. (Periphrastic Expression of the Comparative and Superlative||'')''}}<!-- grrrrrrrrr -->

<div style="font-size: small; text-align: center;">A. Wünsche, ‘Der Komparativ im Hebr. im Lichte der arab. Gramm.,’ in ''Vierteljahrsschrift für Bibelkunde'', 1904, p. 398 ff.</div>

{{GHGmargin-letter|133|a}}
'''1.''' Hebrew possesses no special forms either for the comparative or superlative of the adjective.<ref>There is in Arabic a special form of the adjective (the ''elative'') for the comparative and superlative, which in Hebrew would have the form {{GHGheb|text=אַקְטָל}}. Instances of it, perhaps, are {{GHGheb|text=אַכְזָר|translate=daring, cruel}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַכְזָב|translate=deceptive}} (of a brook drying up), and its opposite {{GHGheb|text=אֵיתָן}} (contracted from ''ʾaitan'') ''constantly flowing'', ''perennis''. These forms are, however, used without any perceptible emphasis, and cannot be regarded as more than isolated relics of an elative formation which has become obsolete, much as the Latin comparative disappears in Italian, and still more so in French, and is supplanted by the circumlocution with ''più'', ''plus''.</ref> In order to express a comparative, the person or thing which is to be represented as excelled in some particular quality is attached to the attributive word by the preposition {{GHGheb|text=מִן־}} ({{GHGheb|text=מִ‍·}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=2}} {{GHGheb|text=גָּבֹהַּ מִכָּל־הָעָם|translate=higher than any of the people}}. The fundamental idea evidently is, ''tall away from all the people'' (beyond all the people); cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=14|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=מַה־מָּתוֹק מִדְּבַשׁ וּמֶה עַז מֵֽאֲרִי|translate=what is sweeter than honey? and what is stronger than a lion?}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=28|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=6|verse=2}}. Frequently an infinitive appears as the object of the comparison, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=19}} ''it is better that I give her to thee, than that I should give her'', &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=14|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=118|verse=8}}f.<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=11|verse=25}} the adjective is specially intensified by repetition, ''art thou so much better than Balak?'' It would also be possible, however, to translate ''art thou really better ...?''</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|133|b}}
Rem. 1. This use of {{GHGheb|text=מִן־}} is also very common when the attributive idea is represented by an intransitive verb, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=23}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּגְבַּהּ מִכָּל־הָעָם|translate=and he was higher than any of the people}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=3|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=7|verse=6}}. Elsewhere, especially after transitive verbs, {{GHGheb|text=מִן־}} rather represents (on its different senses see {{GHGpar|119|v}}–{{GHGpar|119|z|nonumber=1}}) the idea<section end=par133 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>
